title: Applications of Gauss's Theorem in Electrostatics and Gravitation
short_intro: Gauss's theorem relates the surface integral of a vector field over a closed surface to the source enclosed within that surface. It simplifies the evaluation of electric and gravitational fields for highly symmetrical distributions.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Direct application of Gauss's law for symmetric charge distributions (infinite line charge, infinite plane sheet, spherical shell), finding electric field and potential.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Differential form of Gauss's law (divergence theorem application), gravitational field and potential analogues, Poisson's and Laplace's equations, and non-uniform volume distributions.

prerequisites: Concept of electric and gravitational flux

concept_notes.heading: Statement of Gauss's Law in Electrostatics
bullets: The total electric flux through any closed Gaussian surface is equal to 1/ε<sub>0</sub> times the net charge enclosed by the surface.
Only the charges enclosed within the Gaussian surface contribute to the net flux on the left-hand side, whereas the electric field E is due to all charges both inside and outside.
The Gaussian surface must be a closed, continuous surface chosen to exploit the symmetry of the charge distribution.

concept_notes.heading: Gravitational Analogue of Gauss's Law
bullets: In gravitation, the flux of the gravitational field intensity g through a closed surface is equal to -4πG times the total mass enclosed.
The negative sign arises due to the attractive nature of gravitational forces compared to repulsive/attractive electrostatic forces between like/unlike charges.

concept_notes.heading: Differential Form of Gauss's Law
bullets: Relates the local behavior of a vector field to its source density at any point in space using the divergence operator.
For electrostatics, ∇ · E = ρ/ε<sub>0</sub>, where ρ is the volume charge density.
For gravitation, ∇ · g = -4πGρ<sub>m</sub>, where ρ<sub>m</sub> is the mass density.

concept_notes.heading: Symmetry Conditions for Application
bullets: Spherical symmetry allows the choice of a concentric spherical Gaussian surface where E is constant in magnitude and normal to the surface.
Cylindrical symmetry permits a coaxial cylindrical Gaussian surface for line charges or long cylinders.
Planar symmetry uses a pillbox Gaussian surface intersecting a sheet of charge perpendicularly.

derivations.title: Electric Field due to an Infinite Uniformly Charged Line
derivations.conditions: Infinite length, uniform linear charge density λ, cylindrical symmetry
steps: Choose a coaxial cylindrical Gaussian surface of radius r and length l.
Evaluate the electric flux through the surface: flux through flat end faces is zero because E is perpendicular to dA; flux through the curved surface is E(2πrl).
Equate the total flux to the enclosed charge divided by ε<sub>0</sub>: E(2πrl) = (λl)/ε<sub>0</sub>.

derivations.title: Electric Field due to a Uniformly Charged Thin Spherical Shell
derivations.conditions: Radius R, total charge Q, spherical symmetry
steps: For a point outside the shell (r > R), choose a spherical Gaussian surface of radius r. Flux = E(4πr<sup>2</sup>) = Q/ε<sub>0</sub>.
For a point inside the shell (r < R), the enclosed charge is zero because charge resides entirely on the surface.
Equate flux for internal point: E(4πr<sup>2</sup>) = 0, giving zero internal electric field.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Electric Field vs Distance for a Charged Conducting Sphere
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A graph with E on the y-axis and r on the x-axis. E is zero from r = 0 to r = R, jumps discontinuously at r = R, and falls off as 1/r<sup>2</sup> for r > R.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Discontinuity at the boundary r = R equals σ/ε<sub>0</sub>, representing the surface charge layer.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently asked in MCQ format to identify correct field profiles for conductors vs non-conductors.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Electric Field vs Distance for a Solid Non-Conducting Sphere
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: E increases linearly from r = 0 to r = R (E ∝ r), reaching a maximum at r = R, then decreases non-linearly (E ∝ 1/r<sup>2</sup>) for r > R.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Illustrates how internal enclosed charge grows proportionally with volume (r<sup>3</sup>), while the 1/r<sup>2</sup> geometric factor causes the field to drop outside.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested via conceptual matching questions on volumetric scaling.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Cavendish Torsion Balance Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Schematic setup of two small spheres attached to a light rod suspended by a torsion fiber, influenced by two large lead spheres.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Measures the weak gravitational force between laboratory masses, confirming the inverse-square law underpinning gravitational Gauss's law.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Asked in descriptive or historical context relating to the determination of G and Earth's mass.

solved_numericals.question: A point charge q is placed at the center of a cube of side a. What is the electric flux passing through one face of the cube?
solution_steps: Total electric flux through all 6 faces of the cube according to Gauss's law is Φ<sub>total</sub> = q / ε<sub>0</sub>.
Due to the symmetrical placement of the charge at the center, the flux is distributed equally across all 6 identical faces.

solved_numericals.question: The electric field in a region is given by E = 3x^2 i + 4j N/C. Find the total charge enclosed within a cube defined by x = 0 to 2 m, y = 0 to 2 m, and z = 0 to 2 m.
solution_steps: Use the differential form of Gauss's law: ∇ · E = ρ / ε<sub>0</sub>, or Q<sub>enclosed</sub> = ε<sub>0</sub> ∫ (∇ · E) dV.
Integrate over the volume of the cube: Q<sub>enclosed</sub> = ε<sub>0</sub> ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>2</sup> ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>2</sup> ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>2</sup> (6x) dx dy dz.
Multiply by y and z limits (each of length 2): Q<sub>enclosed</sub> = ε<sub>0</sub> × 12 × 2 × 2 = 48ε<sub>0</sub>.

solved_numericals.question: A solid non-conducting sphere of radius R has a non-uniform volume charge density given by ρ = ρ<sub>0</sub>(r/R), where r is the distance from the center. Find the electric field at a distance r (r < R).
solution_steps: Set up Gauss's law for a spherical Gaussian surface of radius r (r < R): ∮ E · dA = E(4πr<sup>2</sup>) = Q<sub>enclosed</sub> / ε<sub>0</sub>.

Calculate enclosed charge by integrating volume charge density: Q<sub>enclosed</sub> = ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>r</sup> ρ(r) (4πr<sup>2</sup>) dr = ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>r</sup> (ρ<sub>0</sub> r / R) (4πr<sup>2</sup>) dr.
Q<sub>enclosed</sub> = (4πρ<sub>0</sub> / R) ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>r</sup> r<sup>3</sup> dr = (4πρ<sub>0</sub> r<sup>4</sup>) / (4R) = πρ<sub>0</sub> r<sup>4</sup> / R.
Equate to flux: E(4πr<sup>2</sup>) = (πρ<sub>0</sub> r<sup>4</sup>) / (ε<sub>0</sub> R).
Solve for E: E = ρ<sub>0</sub> r<sup>2</sup> / (4ε<sub>0</sub> R).

assumptions_and_limitations: Gauss's law is universally valid for any inverse-square central force field, but it is only practically useful for calculating fields when high spatial symmetry (spherical, cylindrical, or planar) allows E to be factored out of the surface integral.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The electric field on a Gaussian surface is determined solely by the charges enclosed inside it.
common_misconceptions.correct: The electric field at any point on the Gaussian surface is the vector sum of fields produced by all charges, both inside and outside the surface.
common_misconceptions.why: While outside charges integrate to zero net flux over a closed surface, they still contribute to the local value of the electric field vector at specific points on the surface.

common_misconceptions.wrong: A Gaussian surface must be a physical boundary made of a real material.
common_misconceptions.correct: A Gaussian surface is purely mathematical and imaginary.
common_misconceptions.why: It can be chosen arbitrarily in empty space to match the symmetry of the physical problem.

quick_revision: Gauss's theorem connects total flux through a closed surface to the enclosed source divided by ε<sub>0</sub> (or -4πG for gravity).
Integral Form of Gauss's Law (Electrostatics): \oint \mathbf{E} \cdot d\mathbf{A} = \frac{Q_{enclosed}}{\varepsilon_0}
